text: I’ll model a 0.040 m sphere centered at the origin inside a rectangular external-flow domain: \(x=[-0.20,0.60]\) m and \(y,z=[-0.20,0.20]\) m. I’ll use `blockMesh` for a coarse background grid and `snappyHexMesh` for sphere fitting, local refinement, and prism layers. First I’ll create and measure the sphere, export its named surface, and inspect it visually.

The sphere is dimensionally correct and visually closed. I’ll now create the coarsest background mesh at 20 mm nominal spacing (16,000 hexahedra), with inlet, outlet, and all four lateral boundaries grouped as `farField`. This is intentionally coarse; sphere resolution and layers will be added only after this domain is checked.
`blockMesh` found the dictionary but OpenFOAM requires a minimal `system/controlDict` even for meshing utilities. I’ll add that case metadata and rerun the same coarse mesh.

The coarse mesh has the intended 20 mm cells, 16,000 cells total, and correctly separated domain patches. I’ll inspect it in a center-plane cut together with the sphere surface to verify placement and extents before configuring refinement.

The center cut confirms the requested clearances and sphere placement. For the fitted mesh I’ll use three refinement levels at the sphere, giving a 2.5 mm near-surface Cartesian scale (16 cells per diameter before snapping), then request five prism layers with 1.2 expansion and a final layer thickness of 30% of the local cell size. These layer settings are meshing assumptions because no target \(y^+\), Reynolds number, or first-cell height was specified.
I’ll now run `snappyHexMesh` on the checked background grid and inspect its stage summary, especially whether all five requested layers were actually added rather than merely configured.

This OpenFOAM build also requires placeholder `fvSchemes` and `fvSolution` dictionaries during mesh creation. I’ll add empty valid dictionaries; they contain no solver setup or boundary conditions, then rerun the mesher.

The utility validates the standard discretization sub-dictionaries even though it does not solve equations. I’ll provide minimal `default none`/standard geometry entries solely to satisfy that parser and rerun.

Meshing succeeded with 24,488 cells. All 744 sphere faces received all five layers (3,720 prism cells total), with a reported total layer thickness of 2.69 mm. I’ll now run the full OpenFOAM topology and geometry checks.

The exhaustive optional check reports 519 concave polyhedral cells around the snapped/layered sphere, while all primary quality metrics are good (max non-orthogonality 35.7°, max skewness 0.535, positive volumes, one region). Concavity is common in valid snappy polyhedra but I will not rely on that alone; I’ll run the standard binding `checkMesh` test next.

The standard check passes: `Mesh OK`, one connected fluid region, four named patches, positive volumes, and strong quality margins. I’ll make a close-up center-plane inspection to verify the fitted sphere and visible layered near-wall structure, and independently measure the final sphere patch bounds.

The numeric inspection confirms a 39.995–40.000 mm fitted diameter and the correct patch names, but the close-up camera framing was blank. I’ll correct the view and redraw the center cut so the layer structure is actually visible rather than treating the failed image as evidence.

The corrected inspection clearly shows five continuous near-wall layers around the sphere. The clean rebuild reproduces all 24,488 cells and 100% five-layer coverage. I’ll perform one final standard mesh check on that rebuilt result and record the concise quality figures used for handoff.
